question: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?
answer:
Based on the sections I read, these are three related features. Tracing data appears in the Agents view, Signals add tags and ratings there, and evaluations run an `Evaluation` over a `Dataset`. The one explicit link I found is that conversation messages can be added to a `Dataset`.

- **Tracing (the activity record):** The Agents view gives a turn-by-turn record of agent conversations, including token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans [S3].
- **Signals (tags and ratings):** The Signals tab in the Agents view shows tags and ratings for conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues and highlight the traces that need attention [S1]. A rating is a numeric score from 0.0 to 1.0 assigned to a matching span. Tags are labels, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw", assigned to matching spans [S4].
- **Evaluations (curated test examples):** An `Evaluation` object defines a `Dataset` or list of examples plus scoring functions. Each `.evaluate()` call runs it against a `Model` or function as an evaluation run [S2]. The docs describe this as measuring behavior against consistent, curated examples [S2].

**The connection:** In the Agents view, **Add to dataset** adds selected conversation messages to a `Dataset` [S5]. An `Evaluation` can use a `Dataset` for its examples [S2]. So traced conversations could feed evaluation data.

**Limits of this answer:** I read only a few sections of these pages. I didn't find a documented end-to-end workflow that ties tracing, Signals, and evaluations together. I also didn't establish how Signals relate to evaluation scorers. I used the Agents/Signals pages and didn't blend in the legacy Monitors docs.

# View agent activity

> Use Weave's Agents view to understand what your agent did, how much it cost, and exactly where things went right or wrong.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/conversations/view-activity.md).

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. You can see at a glance whether an agent completed its task, how many tool calls it made, and where time or budget was spent. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

* **Turn**: One back-and-forth exchange between the user and the agent.
* **Rating**: A numeric score between 0.0 and 1.0 assigned to a matching span.
* **Tags**: Labels assigned to matching spans, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw".

sources.heading: Evaluations overview
sources.text:
# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

sources.heading: Add agent messages to a dataset
sources.text:
#### Add agent messages to a dataset

To add agent messages to a `Dataset`:

1. In the conversation details panel header, click **Add to dataset** to open the **Add example to dataset** drawer.
2. In **Choose a dataset**, use the dropdown to choose the dataset you want to add traces to.
3. In **Select context**, select which messages to add to the dataset. Click **Next**.
4. Review your selections and click **Add to dataset**.

> Use Weave's Agents view to understand what your agent did, how much it cost, and exactly where things went right or wrong.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/conversations/view-activity.md).

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. You can see at a glance whether an agent completed its task, how many tool calls it made, and where time or budget was spent. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

#### Add agent messages to a dataset

To add agent messages to a `Dataset`:

1. In the conversation details panel header, click **Add to dataset** to open the **Add example to dataset** drawer.
2. In **Choose a dataset**, use the dropdown to choose the dataset you want to add traces to.
3. In **Select context**, select which messages to add to the dataset. Click **Next**.
4. Review your selections and click **Add to dataset**.

results.title: View agent activity
results.heading: Get started
results.snippet:
## Get started

To open the Agents view for your project:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.
2. In the sidebar menu, select **Agents** to view all agent conversations saved for your project.

The Agents view is organized into a row of tabs across the top: **Dashboard**, **Agents**, **Conversations**, **Spans**, and **Signals**. The **Dashboard** tab gives a project-wide overview of agent activity, while the other tabs let you drill into individual agents, conversations, spans, and signals.

results.title: Monitor your agents with signals
results.heading: Manage and edit signals
results.snippet:
## Manage and edit signals

If you have at least one created signal, select the active signals button in the toolbar—labeled with the number of active signals, such as **1 active signals**—to open a drawer that lists all active signals for the project. From there you can toggle signals on or off, delete them, or edit any signal. The editor shows the same configuration fields as a custom signal.

results.title: Monitor using built-in signals
results.heading: Manage active signals
results.snippet:
## Manage active signals

After your signals are running, you can review which ones are active or turn off signals you no longer need. To view or remove active signals:

1. From the Monitors page, select the **Manage signals** () button. This opens a drawer listing all currently active signals grouped by category.
2. Hover over a signal and select the **Remove signal** () button to deactivate the signal.

Removing a signal stops scoring new traces. Weave preserves existing scores from the signal.

results.title: View agent activity
results.heading: Signals tab
results.snippet:
## Signals tab

The **Signals** tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

For setup and detailed usage, see [Monitor your agents with signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

results.heading: Custom signals
results.snippet:
### Custom signals

To create a custom tag signal from an empty Signals tab, see [Create a custom signal](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/create-custom-signal.md).

results.title: Monitor using built-in signals
results.heading: Available signals
results.snippet:
## Available signals

Weave offers monitors with built-in signals: preset scorers that evaluate production traces for common quality issues and errors by default, with no custom setup. Each built-in signal uses a benchmarked LLM prompt to classify traces and saves the results as comma-delimited tags representing the detected issues.

Signals use a [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) model to score traces, so you don't need external API keys.

Weave provides 13 preset signals organized into two groups.

# Scoring overview

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

This guide is for developers who want to measure the quality of their AI system's outputs. It explains how Scorers fit into Weave evaluations, how to build your own Scorers, how to apply Scorers to individual calls, and how to analyze the resulting scores.

**Python**

Pass Scorers to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation. Weave supports two types of Scorers:

1. **Function-based Scorers:** Python functions decorated with `@weave.op`.
2. **Class-based Scorers:** Python classes that inherit from `weave.Scorer` for more complex evaluations.

Scorers must return a dictionary and can return multiple metrics, nested metrics, and non-numeric values such as text returned from an LLM-evaluator about its r

result.title: Evaluations overview
result.heading: Evaluations overview
result.text:
# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

input.answer:
In the Agents/Signals workflow, tracing records what your agent did, Signals score or tag that recorded activity in production, and evaluations are a separate, test-driven workflow that uses curated examples. The snapshot I searched doesn't describe one unified pipeline across all three, so the links below are only the ones the docs state.

- **Tracing (the data):** The Agents view gives a turn-by-turn record of agent conversations, including token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans [S3].
- **Signals (production scoring):** Signals appear in the Agents view's Signals tab as tags and ratings for conversations. They flag quality and safety issues and highlight the traces that need attention [S1]. A rating is a numeric score from 0.0 to 1.0 on a matching span. Tags are labels such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw" [S4].
- **Evaluations (repeatable testing):** An `Evaluation` object defines a `Dataset` or list of examples plus scoring functions. Each `.evaluate()` call runs it against a `Model` or function as an evaluation run [S2]. The docs describe this as measuring behavior against consistent, curated examples [S2].

**Where they connect:** In the Agents view you can use **Add to dataset** to add conversation messages to a `Dataset` [S5]. The evaluations page names `Dataset` as a source of test examples [S2].
